q: The technician counts the lifejackets with you: eight for eight people. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: Two child lifejackets sized by weight, plus a spare adult one
o: Nothing — eight jackets for eight people is the rule
Two more adult jackets, straps pulled tight for the children
A note on the form that the children stay in the cockpit
why: One lifejacket per person of the right size, plus spares; an adult jacket slides straight off a child.

fig.title: Lifejackets, cockpit locker
lines: Crew list: 6 adults, 2 children (24 kg, 31 kg)

q: You open the cover of one inflatable lifejacket and find this. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to service or replace the jackets before you leave
o: Screw the cylinder home by hand and sign — the rest is cosmetic
Pull the toggle to prove it inflates, then sign the form
Accept them — a jacket is only serviced after it has been used
why: Loose cylinder, red indicator, overdue service: the jacket may not inflate. The base replaces it, you note it.

q: You plan an overnight passage to Kos. What do you do about this before you sign?
a: Ask for new webbing and a tether, rig the jackstays and test each clip
o: Leave them in the locker — the Dodecanese is coastal sailing
Rig them as they are; the webbing is only used in daylight
Run a mooring line along the deck instead and sign for them
why: You clip on at night and in a sea; faded webbing and a bent hook will not hold a fall.

fig.title: Harnesses and jackstays
lines: Stowed in the locker, not rigged

q: The technician says the liferaft 'is fine, nobody has ever opened it'. What do you do?
a: Refuse to sail until an in-date raft is aboard
o: Accept it — a raft is only serviced after inflation
Take it, but note the date on the form in case
Ask for a second raft to make up for the old one
why: A raft past its service date may not inflate; an expired raft means you do not leave the pontoon.

q: The raft is in date. You look at the cradle on the coachroof. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: An 8-person raft, painter made fast, padlock swapped for a quick-release
o: A second 6-person raft, with its painter tied to the first
The padlock key kept at the chart table, noted on the form
Nothing — six is enough: the dinghy takes the other two
why: Raft capacity covers everyone aboard; the painter is tied on, and the lashings open by hand or hydrostatic release.

fig.title: Liferaft in its cradle
lines: Painter: coiled in the cradle, not tied

q: You check the flares in the container against the base's list. What goes on the form?
a: In date: 0 parachute, 2 hand, 2 smoke — base to make up the list
o: 6 flares as counted — the dates are the base's responsibility
2 parachute, 2 hand, 2 smoke — the list is for bigger yachts
4 in date — expired flares still fire, only less reliably
why: Only in-date flares count; write the real count on the form and the base makes up the shortfall before departure.

q: You walk the boat with the base's list of fire gear. What do you ask for?
a: Aft cabin extinguisher replaced, one at the engine port, a fire blanket
o: Nothing — the galley extinguisher covers a 45 ft monohull
The aft cabin one shaken hard — settled powder lifts the gauge
A bucket on a lanyard by the galley instead of a blanket
why: Count, type, gauge in the green and service date per extinguisher; the engine port needs its own, the galley its blanket.

fig.title: Fire gear, base's list: 3 extinguishers
lines: Aft cabin: 1 kg powder, gauge red, 2022
Engine bay: fire port, no extinguisher beside it

q: The technician hands you a new fire blanket and asks where you want it. Where does it go?
a: By the galley, reachable without leaning over the stove
o: In the engine bay, next to the extinguisher port
In the forepeak, with the spare sails and the tools
In the cockpit locker, together with the flares
why: A blanket is for a pan or stove fire: mounted beside the galley, on the side away from the flames.

q: You press the EPIRB's test button and read the label. What do you do?
a: Ask for a replacement — battery expired, self-test fails
o: Write 'EPIRB tested' on the form — the light is just weak
Take it — in an emergency you would use the VHF first
Pull the sea switch to prove it transmits, then sign
why: Registration, battery date and a passed self-test are the three checks; a dead EPIRB is replaced, never 'tested live'.

fig.title: EPIRB, bracket by the companionway
lines: Registered: this yacht, MMSI on the label

q: You open the first-aid kit against the inventory list. What do you do?
a: List the missing and expired items on the form; the base restocks it
o: Sign — you will buy what you need at the pharmacy in town
Sign — a first-aid kit is a courtesy, not an inventory item
Take the whole kit ashore and bring your own instead
why: The kit is inventory: contents and dates are checked, shortfalls are written down and made up by the base.

q: At the pushpit the technician shows you the horseshoe. You picture this moment on Monday. What do you ask for?
a: The horseshoe on a quick-release clip, with a light and a danbuoy
o: The horseshoe lashed tighter so a sea cannot take it
A second horseshoe at the bow for a bow-first pick-up
Nothing — the fenders float and are quicker to throw
why: MOB gear goes in seconds: horseshoe and danbuoy on a quick release, a light for the night, a throwing line within reach.

fig.note: Horseshoe lashed on with a knot · no light · no danbuoy

q: The technician points at the emergency tiller under the bunk and moves on. What do you do?
a: Open the deck plate and fit it on the rudder stock yourself, now
o: Note where it is kept — fitting it is for an emergency
Ask the technician to confirm it fits, and sign
Lash it in the cockpit so it is ready when needed
why: Find it and try it: a tiller that does not fit, or a plate that will not open, is found at the base, not in a gale.

fig.title: Emergency tiller
lines: Found: under the aft cabin bunk
Rudder-stock plate: cockpit sole, aft of the wheel

q: You lift the floorboards with the technician and find this. What do you ask for?
a: A bung tied to each seacock and the manual pump handle
o: Nothing — the electric pump works and the bungs are aboard
A spare electric pump in place of the manual one
The bungs hammered into the seacocks now, to be ready
why: A bung lives tied to its seacock; the manual pump needs its handle in place — power is the first thing to go.

fig.title: Below the floorboards
lines: Bag of softwood bungs: chart table
Electric bilge pump: runs on test

q: This is what the safety locker holds against the base's list. What goes on the form?
a: Bolt cutters, a full foghorn and spare batteries — base to supply
o: Nothing — a knife, a phone light and AIS cover all of these
The foghorn only — the rest is for offshore boats
The bolt cutters only — the rest you can buy in town
why: Cutters or a rigging knife for a lost mast, a working horn, a torch with spares; the grab bag you pack yourself.

q: Two of your crew are weak swimmers. Before you leave you ask the technician how a person in the water gets back aboard. What answer do you want?
a: The bathing ladder drops from the water and a spare halyard reaches a cockpit winch to hoist someone up
o: The crew pull the casualty in over the guardrail together
The dinghy is launched and the casualty climbs into it
The liferaft is thrown to the casualty as a float
why: Recovery is planned at the base: a ladder that opens from the water and a halyard to a winch for someone who cannot climb; try both.

fig.title: Getting back aboard
lines: Bathing ladder: folds down from the platform
Spare halyard: topping lift to a cockpit winch

q: The base manager reads out the emergency numbers at the briefing. Where do they go?
a: On a card by the VHF and in your phone, before you leave
o: In the ship's log, to look up when they are needed
In the base's folder — it stays aboard anyway
In your head — three numbers are easy to remember
why: Channel 16, the base's phone and the local emergency number: written where any crew member can find them.

fig.title: Base briefing — numbers
lines: Base office: phone on the key fob

q: The technician shrugs: 'the lifebuoy light is extra, nobody checks it'. What do you do?
a: Ask for the light — the base's list is the law's minimum for the boat
o: Take his word for it — the base knows the local rules
Buy a light in town and claim it back from the deposit
Cross the light off the list before you sign the form
why: The base's list is the national equipment regulation for the flag; every item on it is aboard before you sign.

q: The raft cannot be swapped before Monday. What do you do?
a: Stay at the base until a serviced raft is aboard; note it on the form
o: Sail Sunday inside the Ionian and come back Monday for the raft
Sail with the dinghy inflated on deck in place of the raft
Sign for the boat and ask for a discount instead of a raft
why: Out-of-date safety gear is replaced before you leave; the base's problem does not become your crew's risk.

q: The boat is signed for and the crew are aboard. What do you do before supper?
a: Walk them through lifejackets, MOB, gas, heads and who does what
o: Let them settle in — the briefing is better once under way
Brief the two who have sailed; they pass it on to the rest
Show them the lifejackets; the rest is covered on the first sail
why: Your own safety briefing before leaving: jackets and where they are, MOB, gas and heads, swim rules, jobs.

q: The technician shows you the swim ladder. What rule do you set for your crew before anyone swims?
a: Engine off and key out, ladder down, then into the water
o: Engine in neutral, ticking over to charge the batteries
Engine off, ladder up so nobody climbs near the propeller
Lifejackets on for everyone who goes in the water
why: A turning propeller kills; a ladder down means a tired swimmer can get back aboard.

q: You read the lifejacket labels while the crew are still at the airport. What do you ask the base for?
a: Auto-inflating jackets with spray hoods for the non-swimmers and the child
o: Nothing — a manual toggle is easier for a child to find
Manual jackets for everyone, with a demonstration of the toggle
One auto jacket for the helm; the rest stay in the cabin
why: A stunned or weak swimmer cannot pull a toggle; auto inflation and a spray hood keep the airway clear in a sea.

fig.title: Lifejackets, 6 of 6
lines: Crew: two non-swimmers, one child of 9

q: Reading the form again on Sunday morning you write your lifejacket rule for the week. Which one?
a: Children always on deck; everyone at night, when reefed, and in the dinghy
o: Everyone until the first swim stop, then as each one likes
Children only; adults decide for themselves when to wear one
Only when the base's wind limit is reached, as the contract says
why: The skipper sets the rule before leaving: children whenever out of the cabin, all hands at night, in a reef and in the dinghy.

q: The technician walks the side deck with you. With two small children coming aboard, what do you ask for?
a: Netting on the guardrails and two child harnesses, gates clipped shut
o: Nothing — the children stay below while the boat is moving
Adult harnesses on the shortest setting and the gates tied open
A second guardrail wire run at knee height instead of netting
why: A child slides under a guardrail wire: netting, a harness that fits and closed gates are the base's job before you leave.

q: Tuesday, 23:00, at anchor off Fiskardo. Two crew want to take the dinghy ashore for a drink. What do you insist on?
a: Lifejackets on, a torch, kill cord on the wrist and a time to be back
o: Oars only — the outboard is too loud for the anchorage at night
A lifejacket for the one who drives; the passenger holds the torch
Nothing — 300 m is a short run and the outboard is reliable
why: A dinghy at night is where charter crews drown: jackets worn, a light to be seen, the kill cord on, and the skipper knows when they are due.

q: Your crew ask how the liferaft is actually launched. What do you tell them?
a: Check the painter is tied on, throw the canister to leeward, pull the painter until it fires, board dry
o: Throw the canister to windward so the raft drifts back to the boat
Open the canister on deck, inflate the raft and lower it over the side
Throw the canister, swim to it and pull the painter from the water
why: Painter made fast to the yacht, canister over the lee side, a sharp pull on the painter inflates it; step in dry, cut the painter last.

q: Monday, motoring out of Alimos, smoke comes from the engine box under the companionway steps. What is the drill you set on Saturday?
a: Stop the engine, fuel and gas off, extinguisher through the port, bay kept shut
o: Open the engine box, find the flame and aim the extinguisher at it
Keep the engine running to reach the quay, then fight the fire
Pour sea water down the step while someone calls the base
why: Opening the bay feeds the fire with air; through the port the powder fills the space while fuel and gas are cut and the crew get ready to call.

fig.title: Engine fire drill
lines: Fire port: on the step panel, cap on
Gas valve: at the bottle, cockpit locker
Fuel shut-off: by the engine panel

q: The 36 ft boat has no fire port. The technician says the engine is 'right under the steps anyway'. What do you ask for and plan?
a: A second extinguisher by the companionway; lift the step a crack and aim through the gap
o: Nothing — on a small boat one extinguisher in the forecabin is enough
A port drilled in the step by the base before you leave on Sunday
The forecabin extinguisher moved to the engine box, inside the lid
why: Without a port you open the box the least you can and discharge through the crack; the extinguisher lives where the fire is fought, not in the bow.

fig.title: Engine access, 36 ft
lines: Engine box: lifts with the companionway steps

q: You find this in the cockpit locker. The technician says 'they are all together, easier to count'. What do you ask?
a: Each one mounted in its bracket — galley, companionway, aft cabin — before you sign
o: Nothing — three in date, counted and photographed, is the check
Two in the locker and one by the wheel, where the skipper sits
All three by the engine, where a boat fire usually starts
why: A fire below is fought from where you are, with the extinguisher at hand: one by each escape route and the galley, not in a locker on deck.

q: The EPIRB passes its self-test. You read the label against the boat's papers. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to swap it for this yacht's own EPIRB, or re-register it, before you leave
o: Nothing — the beacon transmits a position whatever name it carries
Stick the boat's name over the label and note it on the form
Take it — the base's phone number is what the rescue centre uses
why: A beacon alerts under its registration: rescuers look for the wrong yacht, crew and base contact. The base fixes the registration, not you.

fig.title: EPIRB label
lines: MMSI: not the one on the radio licence

q: Friday evening at anchor, last night of the week. Your crew find the expired flares the base left aboard and want a show. What do you say?
a: No — a red flare is a distress signal; the expired ones go back to the base for disposal
o: Yes, the smoke only — orange is not a distress colour at night
Yes, one handheld well away from the other boats, as practice
Yes, if you call the coastguard first so they do not come out
why: Any red flare means distress and launches a rescue; expired pyrotechnics are returned to the base, never fired for fun or practice.

fig.title: Flares aboard
lines: 3 expired — in a bag, 'for the base'

q: Saturday evening, the crew unpack. One of them hands you this list. What do you do with it?
a: Write it on your crew sheet, stow each medicine where you both know, tell the co-skipper
o: Keep it to yourself — medical details are private aboard
Ask them to manage it themselves; your job is the boat
File it with the base's papers so the office has it
why: The skipper knows who takes what and where it is, and a second person knows too, so a collapse at sea is not a mystery.

q: Sunday, 08:00, departure at nine. A crew member who has never sailed asks when to take the seasickness tablet. What do you tell him?
a: Now, with breakfast — an hour before leaving, then stay on deck and take the helm
o: When he first feels queasy — before that it is wasted
Not at all — tablets make him drowsy and useless on the winch
After an hour at sea, once he knows whether he needs it
why: Tablets work only if taken before the motion starts; food, fresh air, the horizon and a job at the wheel do the rest.

fig.title: Sunday morning
lines: Forecast: F4–5 on the nose, short sea
Tablets: in the first-aid kit, in date

q: Monday, the genoa sheet runs through a crew member's palm during a tack. The first-aid kit is as restocked on Saturday. What do you do?
a: Cool it under fresh water for 15–20 minutes, then a burn dressing, loosely bandaged
o: Rinse it in sea water and let the sun dry it out
Cover it in antiseptic cream and tape it tight so he can winch
Ice from the fridge straight on the skin until it goes numb
why: A rope burn is a burn: cool with fresh water, cover with a clean non-stick dressing; no cream, no ice, no sea water in an open wound.

fig.title: Rope burn, right palm
lines: Skin red and raw across the palm
Kit: burn dressings, sterile water, bandages

q: Your crew gather for the safety briefing. One of them says he has sailed for twenty years and goes below. What do you do?
a: Call him back — the gear and its places are this boat's, and he may be the one who needs them
o: Let him go — an experienced hand will find things when needed
Make him give the briefing instead, since he knows the drills
Skip the briefing — with an old hand aboard you have backup
why: The briefing is about this boat: where the gas valve, the raft and the jackets are and who does what. Experience elsewhere does not cover it.

fig.title: Saturday 19:30, briefing
lines: His boat: a tiller 30-footer, no gas, no raft
This boat: 45 ft, gas, raft on the coachroof
Jackets: a type he has not used

q: Going through the companionway with the technician you check what closes the boat in a sea. What do you ask for?
a: The second washboard with a lanyard, the hatch dog fixed and the seal replaced
o: Nothing — in the Med you sail with the companionway open anyway
A sheet of plywood cut to size, kept in the lazarette for storms
The forehatch taped shut for the week; the rest is fine
why: Washboards and hatches are what keep a knockdown or a boarding sea out of the boat: both boards, tied on, and dogs that close.

fig.title: Companionway and hatches
lines: Washboards: one of two, no lanyard
Companionway hatch: slides, no lock from inside

q: The base's grab bag turns out to be an empty dry bag. Sunday morning you fill it yourself. What goes in?
a: Handheld VHF, flares, torch, water, the papers, the medicines, phone in a dry pouch
o: The passports only — everything else is replaced by the base
The liferaft's own pack is enough; the bag is for valuables
Food for a week, the chart folio and the ship's log
why: The bag goes into the raft with you: a way to call and be seen, water, documents, the crew's medicines, a phone; packed before leaving.

fig.title: Grab bag — your list
lines: Boat: handheld VHF, EPIRB on its bracket
Papers: passports, boat papers in the chart table

q: The technician hands you the throwing line in its bag. Your crew ask how it is used. What do you show them?
a: Keep hold of the loop, throw the bag past and upwind of the person, let them grab the line, pull in
o: Tie the bag to the horseshoe and throw both at the person
Take the line out of the bag, coil it, and throw the coil
Throw the bag straight at the person so it lands in their hands
why: Hand loop held, bag thrown beyond the casualty so the line falls across them; it lives in the cockpit, not under the fenders.

fig.title: Throwing line
lines: Floating line, 20 m, in a bag
Bag end: loop for the hand

q: A crew member shows you his own personal locator beacon. What do you tell him?
a: Clip it to his lifejacket and tell his contact which yacht and where he is this week
o: Leave it in the bag — the yacht's EPIRB covers everyone aboard
Register it to the yacht at the base office before you sail
Hand it to you; the skipper holds all the beacons
why: A PLB is personal: worn on the jacket, and the registered contact knows the trip so the rescue centre has the right picture.

q: Your crew ask what to do if the frying pan catches fire. What do you tell them?
a: Gas off at the stove, fire blanket over the pan from the side, leave it covered
o: A pan of water over it, quickly, before it spreads to the curtains
Carry the pan up to the cockpit and throw it over the side
The powder extinguisher straight into the pan from above
why: Water on burning oil explodes into flame; the blanket smothers it, the gas is shut, the pan stays where it is until cold.

q: Your crew ask why the base's equipment list is different from the one they know from home. Whose rules apply to this boat?
a: The flag of the boat — the Croatian regulation on the base's list
o: The skipper's licence country — German rules follow the skipper
The country of the majority of the crew aboard
Whichever is the strictest of the countries represented
why: Safety equipment is required by the flag state of the vessel; the base's list is that regulation for this boat.

q: You find this in the locker. The technician says 'hang it up if it gets foggy'. What do you do?
a: Hoist it under the spreader now and leave it up all week
o: Leave it in the bag — fog is rare in the Ionian in summer
Hoist it only at night, and take it down for sailing by day
Lash it to the pushpit where it is quick to reach
why: A GRP hull barely shows on a ferry's radar: the reflector goes up high at the base and stays there, day and night.

fig.title: Cockpit locker
lines: Radar reflector: folding octahedral, in its bag

q: The technician shows you where the lifejackets live. What do you ask for?
a: Moved to the cockpit locker or by the companionway, one per person, reachable in seconds
o: Left where they are — the forepeak is dry and they stay clean
One in the cockpit for the helm; the rest stay in the bow
Put on now and worn until the crew are used to them
why: Jackets are reached in seconds from the cockpit when it goes wrong, not dug out from under a sail in the bow.

fig.title: Lifejackets found
lines: Forepeak, under the spare genoa and the fenders

q: Your crew ask what the little light and the whistle on the lifejacket are for. What do you tell them?
a: To be found at night — the light is seen, the whistle is heard over the engine
o: To mark the jacket as serviced — the base checks both
To attract the next ferry so it alters course
To be used at the swim stop when the ladder is up
why: A head in the water is invisible at night: the light and the whistle are how the boat finds you; show the crew where they are.

q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician shows you the liferaft. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: The locker cleared so the raft comes out in seconds, nothing stowed on top
o: Nothing — a locker keeps the raft dry and out of the sun
The raft moved to the trampoline, lashed to the crossbeam
The fenders left on top — they float and are useful too
why: A raft under the fenders and the passerelle is not launched in a hurry; its locker holds the raft and nothing else.

fig.title: Liferaft, catamaran
lines: Stowed: cockpit locker under the table
On top: 6 fenders, the passerelle, the hose
Painter: tied to a ring in the locker

q: Thursday, 02:00, on passage to Rhodes. The lazyjack has parted and the crew on watch wants to go forward to clear it. What do you insist on?
a: Clip on before leaving the cockpit, on the high side, and wake you first
o: Go without the tether — it snags on the lazyjacks at the mast
Clip on at the mast once he gets there, so the tether does not drag
Wait till daylight — nobody goes forward at night, whatever breaks
why: Nobody leaves the cockpit at night unclipped or unseen; the jackstays you rigged at the base are for exactly this moment.

fig.title: Night watch, 02:00
lines: He has a tether, clipped nowhere
You are asleep; one other crew below

q: Thursday, 05:30. You have decided to leave this bay now, ahead of Friday's gale; the passage home is forecast as shown. What do you do before the anchor comes up?
a: Reef at anchor, jackstays rigged, everyone in jackets and harnesses, washboards in, hatches dogged, loose gear stowed
o: Shake out the reefs and set full sail to make the most of the morning breeze
Leave the reefing and harnesses until the wind reaches F6 on the way
Keep the washboards out and the forehatch open for air until the sea builds
why: Everything is done in the calm of the bay: a reef, harnesses or a forehatch are hard and dangerous to sort out once the wind arrives.

fig.title: Thursday 05:30, at anchor
lines: Crew: 6, two never sailed in a blow

q: Wednesday, motoring on the 42 ft catamaran, a crew member falls off the transom steps. You come back to him. What do you do before anyone reaches down?
a: Both engines off and the keys out, then bring him to the steps
o: Port engine off — the steps are on the port hull
Both in neutral, ticking over, so you can hold position
Keep steerage on both and let him swim to the steps
why: Two propellers either side of the steps: a catamaran recovers at the transom only with both engines stopped, as in your swim rule.

fig.note: Both engines ahead · recovery at the stern steps

q: Thursday, entering a bay in Croatia, the wheel suddenly turns freely. What do you do?
a: Sails down, engine idle, fit the emergency tiller you tried on Saturday, anchor in the bay and call the base
o: Steer with the sails to the harbour 3 miles on and berth under sail
Send someone to find the tiller while you hold course on the engine
Drop the anchor where you are and wait for the base to send a tow
why: What you tried at the base works now: way off, tiller on the stock, somewhere safe to anchor, then the base; the harbour can wait.

fig.title: Thursday, 16:00
lines: Under full main and genoa, F4
Emergency tiller: tried at check-in, aft cabin

q: Thursday, 22:00: engine dead, drifting onto a lee shore, MAYDAY sent. A ferry's lights appear 2 miles off. Which flare, and how?
a: A parachute first, downwind, then a handheld over the lee side as the ferry closes
o: A handheld aimed at the ferry's bridge so the officer sees it
Both parachutes at once, straight up, then the smoke
The orange smoke first — it lasts longest and is seen furthest
why: Parachute to be seen far off, handheld to be pinpointed; fired downwind over the lee side, never at a vessel, and night is no time for smoke.

q: Tuesday, 14:00, motoring in no wind at 36 °C. Your crew report this about the one who was on the foredeck all morning. What do you do?
a: Into the shade now, cool him with wet cloths and fanning, sips of water, and call for medical advice
o: A swim stop — the sea cools him faster than anything
Send him to his bunk to sleep it off till the harbour
A cold beer and a salt tablet, then back on deck in a hat
why: Hot dry skin and confusion is heatstroke, not tiredness: cool him fast, fluids if he can swallow, and get advice — it kills.

fig.title: Tuesday, 14:00
lines: Drank one small bottle since breakfast
